summary:
Martian Traces

Martian Traces is a project designed to explore, analyze, and map the surface of Mars while supporting safer future landings and scientific exploration.

The project uses NASA data, including CTX and HiRISE surface images, MOLA elevation data, and HRSC terrain information. By combining these datasets, it aims to examine the Martian landscape, identify craters and rocky areas, analyze elevation differences and slopes, and highlight potentially hazardous regions.

The map is intended to help identify suitable landing areas and provide useful information about the surrounding terrain.

The project also proposes a system in which data collected by rovers or other exploration vehicles on the Martian surface could be added to the map. This would help update surface information, support the study of unexplored areas, and provide useful data for future scientific research and exploration missions.

As an additional concept, the project proposes a sensor-supported landing system with adjustable mechanical legs. These sensors could assess nearby ground conditions and help the lander adapt to uneven surfaces.

The main goal is to combine Mars surface exploration, scientific mapping, information gathered by exploration vehicles, and a practical landing-support concept to contribute to safer and more informed future Mars missions.
details: Project Details – Martian Traces Martian Traces aims to support safer future Mars landings through scientific surface mapping and terrain analysis. The project focuses on Jezero Crater and combines NASA datasets to examine craters, rocky areas, elevation differences, slopes, and potentially hazardous landing regions. The project uses NASA Mars Trek and data from CTX, MOLA, HRSC, and HiRISE. These datasets provide different perspectives of the Martian surface and help build a better understanding of the terrain. One of the main challenges is understanding different surface features and elevation conditions together to identify areas that may be more suitable for landing. The project also introduces an innovative concept: a sensor-supported landing system with adjustable mechanical legs. The proposed sensors could evaluate nearby ground conditions and help the lander adapt to uneven terrain. This is a proposed concept for future development. The project combines planetary science, mapping, data analysis, and engineering ideas to contribute to safer and more informed Mars exploration.
